name: Meridian Harbor Crane Operator Rated Jacket
description:
Certified for crane and heavy-lift operations at Meridian Harbor's irradiated cargo terminals, this jacket meets the MH-Rad-3 standard for incidental radiation exposure from Class 2 contaminated freight — the kind of shipping containers arriving from the Great Lakes reclamation zones and the irradiated manufacturing corridors further east. The outer shell is a lead-composite fiber weave bonded to a thermoplastic inner layer, making the jacket heavier than standard work wear but necessary for operators spending 8–12 hour shifts in proximity to hot cargo. High-vis orange panels on the shoulders and sleeves meet harbor safety requirements, and the Harborworks Collective logo — a stylized crane hook — sits on the right chest.

The jacket is designed for the physical demands of crane operation: articulated elbow panels allow full range of motion without breaking the radiation shielding, and the collar is tall and sealed with a magnetic closure that integrates with compatible respirator collars. Augmentation compatibility is a priority given the high rate of cyberware among experienced dock workers — reinforced port-access panels are standard at the wrist and forearm, and the shoulder seams are cut wide to accommodate prosthetic or enhanced arms. A dosimeter strip on the left wrist reads cumulative radiation exposure and changes color at threshold levels. Harborworks issues replacement jackets when the strip reads yellow; most workers wait until red.
cultural_context: Crane operators are a proud and insular group at Meridian Harbor. The jacket is a mark of certification — you can't operate at the hot terminals without it, and you can't get it without the Harborworks Collective sign-off. New workers who show up with clean jackets get watched carefully until they've proven themselves.
story_hooks: A dosimeter strip on a recovered jacket reads far past the red threshold, but the operator's official health records show no radiation events — someone has been falsifying exposure logs.

A shipping container from an unregistered origin point arrives at the harbor rated for crane-operator-level radiation protocols. Whatever's inside is too hot for standard handling, and the manifest says it's food supplies.

The Harborworks Collective is threatening to strike over jacket replacement timelines — operators are being forced to work in degraded protective gear while Harborworks management disputes the dosimeter readings.

physical_description.visual_profile: Heavy-duty industrial jacket with pronounced shoulder width and reinforced structure. Dominates the silhouette with its bulk and authority — a garment that announces its wearer as certified for hazardous work. The high collar and sealed construction give it an almost armor-like presence. Orange hi-vis panels on shoulders and sleeves create visual breaks against the muted base color. Reads as utilitarian and protective rather than fashionable.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the body to accommodate layered undergarments and range of motion for overhead work. Deliberately oversized at the shoulders to fit both baseline and augmented anatomy. Articulated elbow panels create subtle texture breaks that allow flexion without compromising the shell. Wrist cuffs are snug and reinforced. Overall impression is functional rather than flattering.
physical_description.primary_material: Lead-composite fiber weave bonded to thermoplastic inner layer — visibly denser and heavier than standard work wear. The outer shell has a subtle sheen from the composite weave, slightly industrial-looking. The material has weight and presence.
physical_description.texture: Smooth composite shell with a faint cross-hatch weave pattern visible under close inspection. Articulated elbow panels show quilted ribbing for flexibility. Inner thermoplastic layer is sleek and chemical-resistant. Magnetic closure points have subtle metallic texture. The dosimeter strip on the left wrist has a semi-glossy, almost medical appearance.
physical_description.color_scheme: Muted industrial gray base with international-orange hi-vis panels on shoulders and full sleeve stripes. The Harborworks Collective crane-hook logo in metallic gray sits on the right chest. Dosimeter strip in the wrist area starts as a neutral beige/cream, with color-change capability (yellow, red at thresholds).
physical_description.closures: Magnetic snap system running down the center front, integrated with the collar seal for respirator compatibility. Reinforced magnetic points at wrist cuffs. No traditional zippers — the magnetic system is more reliable in contaminated environments and easier to operate with heavy gloves or augmented hands.
distinctive_features: Integrated dosimeter strip on left wrist with color-change radiation threshold indicators
Tall sealed collar with magnetic closure designed to lock with compatible respirator collars
Articulated elbow panels with quilted ribbing for unrestricted overhead motion
Reinforced port-access panels at wrists and forearms for augmentation compatibility
Wide-cut shoulder seams designed to fit prosthetic and enhanced limbs
International-orange hi-vis shoulder and sleeve panels meeting harbor safety standards
Harborworks Collective crane-hook logo in metallic gray on right chest
Lead-composite outer shell with visible weave pattern
Multiple internal pockets with magnetic closures for tools and dosimetry cards
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 functional. The certification requirement and manufacturing standard elevate it above typical Tier 3 work wear, but the utilitarian design and radiation-shielding purpose keep it from Tier 1 luxury. It is valuable specifically within its operational context.
physical_description.cultural_context: This jacket is a credential, not just clothing. Wearing it signals you are certified for hazardous cargo operations at Meridian Harbor — a skilled position with gatekeeping and peer culture. The jacket marks you as part of an insular professional community. Among dock workers, it is worn with pride; outside that context, it reads as industrial worker. The presence of augmentation-accommodation features acknowledges the prevalence of cyberware among experienced operators. A pristine jacket on a new worker draws scrutiny from veterans.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-worn but meticulously maintained. The outer composite shell shows wear patterns consistent with 8–12 hour shifts: scuffing at the wrists, minor stress marks around the elbow articulation, occasional thermal discoloration from proximity to hot cargo. The hi-vis orange may fade slightly. The dosimeter strip is regularly checked and noted — its color progression is a running log of the wearer's exposure history. Most operators replace jackets when the dosimeter hits yellow, but some aggressive or underpaid workers push to red before requesting replacement.
